Driver check for the Condor fleet
At the start of each two week rotation, vehicles are handed to drivers from a paper book in the mechanics
room. The driver signs a waiver. Keys are passed by hand. There is no separate record of who was actually
driving a vehicle at a given time. If something goes wrong, the book is the only evidence, and it depends on
the page being filled in and matching the person who drove.
Spark Technologies will replace that book with a digital record, and add one check when the engine starts.
The mechanic still assigns a vehicle to a driver. The assignment is stored in a system, with the time written
automatically. At ignition, the driver confirms who they are. If that person matches the assignment, the trip
is logged. If there is no match, or no check, a manager sees it and reviews it. The system does not take
action on its own.
The assignment screen needs no new equipment. The only new equipment is the check inside each
vehicle. Condor chooses which kind is fitted. Nothing is installed until that choice is confirmed.

From the book to the screen
Today, at handover
The mechanic hands the keys to the driver listed for that vehicle.
The driver signs a waiver in the book.
The mechanic writes the vehicle, the driver, and the date by hand.
If the keys are passed to someone else, or the vehicle breaks down, there is usually no written
record.
With the driver check
The mechanic opens the assignment screen and links the driver to the vehicle for the rotation.
The system records the time. There is no handwriting.
When the engine starts, the driver confirms who they are, by card tap or by face check.
The system compares that check with the assignment. A match is logged. A mismatch or a missing
check is sent to a manager.

lines.text: Card tap or face check
Both answer the same question: who is in the seat when the engine starts. Spark Technologies
recommends the card tap for the whole fleet. The face check can be tried later on a small group of vehicles
if Condor decides the extra check is worth the cost and the consent process.
Card tap
Each driver carries one personal card, like an office door card. A small reader is fitted where the driver can
reach it from the seat. Before starting, the driver taps the card. The reader sends a unique number to the
GPS tracker already in the vehicle. The tracker records the time and attaches that driver to the trip, speed,
and location it already sends.
The card has no battery. The reader is wired to the tracker, not to the engine computer, so the fit does not
affect the engine. Condor can choose to hold the ignition until a valid tap, or only to record and flag a
missing tap. Flagging first is the safer start, so a driver is not stuck on site because of a reader.
This confirms that a specific card was tapped in a specific vehicle at a specific time. It does not confirm that
the person holding the card is the owner. A simple process for issuing and replacing cards, and a review
when the same problem repeats, covers that gap. Cards can be lost, shared, or left in another vehicle.
If the IMG tracker can already read a driver card, the reader plugs into equipment Condor already has. That
question is item 16 below.
Face check
A small camera faces the driver, usually on the windscreen pillar or the dashboard. It can see a face at
night. A chip in the camera, not a remote server, compares the live face with a photo taken when the driver
was enrolled. Only the result, match or no match, needs to leave the vehicle, unless Condor later asks to
keep images for flagged events. The check can run through the start of the trip, so a change of driver
during a shift can be noticed. A card tap happens once.
A face is harder to hand to someone else than a card. The check can still fail in sun glare, dust on the lens,
or when the face is covered, for example in cold or dusty conditions. Every driver needs one clear photo
before the check works, and a new photo if people change often.
A face image is personal data under Uzbek law. Each driver must agree in writing, and the data must stay
on servers inside Uzbekistan. The camera costs more than a card reader, and the fit takes longer because
the camera needs a clear, stable view of the face.
Recommendation
Start with the card tap across the fleet. It replaces the paper book, it does not use face photos,
and it is quicker to fit. Pilot the face check on a small group of vehicles only if Condor later
decides continuous checking is worth the cost and the written consent.
